newsitem.title: UK: Copper market muddied by "hidden stocks' reports.
newsitem.headline: Copper market muddied by "hidden stocks' reports.

text.p: Volatile movements and uncertainty in the copper market have been exarcabated by reports of large stockpiles of "hidden stocks', which may or may not exist, traders and analysts said.

On Wednesday, the World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS) reported that nearly 600,000 tonnes of non-LME copper may have built up in Netherlands bonded warehouses between 1991 and 1995. However, many were sceptical, saying such a tonnage could not exist given the current tight nature of the LME market as well as the physical sector.
"I do not believe it...You can doubt the LME if you like, but the physical merchant market is another kettle of fish," one trader said.

On the LME cash/threes copper is at an $80 backwardation, with stocks at the lowest since September 1990. This reflects the lack of off-grade copper and scrap, which is trading near to parity to LME, traders noted.

This is because many traders are having to take LME cathode to meet their scrap requirements - something that would not happen if there were substantial tonnages of extra copper. Warehousing sources were also doubtful that such a large tonnage existed.
"Rotterdam is the major port of entry into the European Union, which is now a single market. From Holland, goods then go to German and France and everywhere in the single market," one said.
Also on Wednesday, Bloomsbury Minerals Economics (BME) said stocks in Western exchange warehouses may account for only one-third of the global copper surplus.

Analysts said the possibility that sizeable tonnages of copper have been and may still be hidden from various reporting agencies explains some of the imponderables the 1990s threw up. Reporting of warehouse stocks of non-ferrous metals in recent years, notably in copper, is now becoming an area of growing concern.

"For some time we and others have predicted surplusses in copper, based in data, and they have not happened," Peter Hollands of BME said. "It has got to the stage now that the LME should do something about what is stored in the bonded warehouses...They should address this with great urgency," Ted Arnold of stockbroker Merrill Lynch said.

Traders said various "sleight-of-hand" operations with stocks on and off the LME may have allowed Sumitomo Corp's former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka to operate without discovery for years. In June, Sumitomo fired former head trader Hamanaka after it alleged that he admitted running up losses now put at $2.6 billion in 10 years of unauthorised trading. Hamanaka has since been arrested and was charged on Tuesday with fraud. Looking at the latest WBMS data, BME said it raises more questions than answers, as 600,000 tonnes of copper is a lot of metal to warehouse in total secrecy.
"Not only would 600,000 tonnes of copper be difficult to hide, but it also makes little commercial sense."
And unlike aluminium it cannot be stored outside and covered against the elements with a tarpaulin. Copper has to be stored under certain conditions, Hollands said.

However, the issue of "rogue traders" of the 1990s, when billions of dollars have been lost has needs to be considered. "It is at least a possibility that some of the former employers of various known and unknown "rogue traders' may eventually turn out to be - perhaps unknowingly - still the legimate owners of one or two hundred thousands of tonnes of hidden copper," BME added. The WBMS data suggests there were major tonnages of unreported stock off the LME in the past and this could be reoccuring now, Hollands said.
